claim: RealCompanion is an arXiv preprint (cs.AI) by Arman Behnam, Sunglyoung Kim and Liangwei Yang; v1 submitted 1 Oct 2026, v2 on 2 Oct 2026. No venue or acceptance is listed, so it is not yet peer-reviewed.
The paper was featured on Hugging Face Daily Papers on 2026-10-05 (submitted by first author Arman Behnam), with 268 upvotes when checked on 2026-10-07, under the Quis Lab organization.
quote: "submittedOnDailyAt": "2026-10-05T00:00:00.000Z" ... "upvotes": 268

claim: The dataset is ten real relationships between people and an AI companion: 27,218 messages over up to 120 days.
quote: We release RealCompanion, ten real relationships between people and an AI companion, with 27,218 messages over up to 120 days.

claim: The authors' motivation: real conversations are private, so existing benchmarks use invented people and invented questions.
quote: Testing this needs real conversations, but real conversations are private, so existing benchmarks use invented people and invented questions.

claim: Only 3.4% of people's messages depend on something said earlier, and the needed earlier message is a median of 2,157 messages back.
quote: Only 3.4% of their messages depend on something said earlier, and when one does, the earlier message is usually far away (a median of 2,157 messages back).

claim: Under a stricter reading (removing items whose referent was still visible on screen) the rate of memory demand is 1.3%.
quote: 3.4% [2.5, 4.6] of the messages participants sent carry a verified memory demand under the recorded reading and 1.3% [0.8, 2.1] under the strict one.

claim: Looking at the most recent messages finds the needed one 95.9% of the time overall but only 2.2% of the time when it is far back.
quote: Looking at the most recent messages finds the needed one 95.9% of the time overall, but only 2.2% of the time when it is far back.

claim: Keyword (BM25) search finds a needed distant message in the top five 24.8% of the time, about eleven times recency, but still misses three in four.
quote: Lexical matching finds one eleven times as often, at 0.248, and still misses three in four.

claim: A detector deciding whether a message needs memory performs at roughly chance on real messages (AUROC 0.530).
quote: a detector that reads the probe and its three preceding messages separates the cases at chance. Its AUROC is 0.530 [0.488, 0.572]

claim: Labeling the same earlier messages as 'memories' makes models bring up the past 10 to 14 percentage points more often, even when nothing from the past is needed.
quote: when the same earlier messages are labeled “memories” instead of “earlier messages”, models bring up the past 10 to 14 percentage points more often, even when nothing from the past is needed.

claim: With no context, models never misfire; given ten unselected earlier messages, they bring up the past when it isn't needed 60.8% of the time (29.2% when messages were selected for the probe).
quote: Given no context, models never reach for a past that is absent. Across the 434 cold opens and the 120 probes whose verified locus is none , the misfire rate without context is zero. With context supplied, it rises to 29.2% when the messages were selected for the probe and to 60.8% when ten were supplied without regard to it

claim: 96% of the measured gain from supplying the recorded evidence lands on messages that need no memory, which the authors say shows pooled averages mislead.
quote: so 96% of it lands on probes that need no memory.

claim: Three agent systems (Claude Opus 5.5, Codex GPT-5.6-sol, Antigravity running Gemini 3.8 Flash) were each run three times per participant to rebuild the persona.
quote: Three agent systems, Claude Opus 5.5, Codex GPT-5.6-sol and Antigravity running Gemini 3.8 Flash, each run three times on each of the ten participants.

claim: All three systems reached persona F1 of about 0.69 to 0.70 (table: 0.686, 0.688, 0.701) while tokens processed differed about thirtyfold (546M vs 18M vs 36M). The abstract rounds this to 'F1 0.71'.
quote: All three reach an F1 of 0.69 to 0.70 while the tokens they process differ about thirtyfold, and each agrees with its own repeated runs at 0.93 to 0.95.

claim: Precision (0.56-0.59) well below recall (0.86-0.89): the systems recover what the file holds but add more; about 70-80 extra fields per 100 recovered.
quote: all three add about seventy to eighty further fields for every hundred they recover.

claim: Authors' framing of the over-inference finding.
quote: Third, AI systems read more into a person than the person revealed. Three agent systems rebuild each persona equally well (F1 0.71). They see the person, and then imagine more.

claim: Codex used about 31 times fewer tokens per run than Claude at the same persona F1, and Antigravity about 15 times fewer.
quote: At the same persona F1, Codex processes about 31 fewer tokens per run than Claude, and Antigravity about 15 fewer.

claim: The conversations come from an internal friendship-style companion app with streaks, a habit tracker and mini-games; the companion speaks first on about half of active days.
quote: The corpus comes from an internal AI-companion application in which a user keeps a persistent friendship-style companion.

claim: Participants consented to research use and release; every message was rewritten by a model during anonymization.
quote: The conversations are by ten people using a companion application for their own purposes; all consented to research use and release.

claim: Ethics approval came from the data operator's internal committee, which the authors say is not independent; no institutional review board was involved.
quote: The study and the release were approved by the data operator’s internal ethics committee under its privacy policy and terms of service; that committee is not independent of the operator, and no institutional review board was involved.

claim: Despite anonymization, a language model matched a writing sample to the right participant's history 98% of the time (chance 10%); a style-only classifier, 83%.
quote: a stylometric classifier using no content words matches them at 83.0% and a language model at 98.0%, against a chance rate of 10%

claim: Authors' own limitation: ten self-selected users of one app are not a sample of companion users, and results may not transfer to other products.
quote: Ten people used one application over four months. They chose that product, so they are not a sample of companion users and still less of people, and the application frames the relationship in a particular way; how much of what is reported here survives a different product is unknown.

claim: Two heaviest users hold 73% of all messages; under the strict reading, five of ten participants contribute no memory-needing items.
quote: The two heaviest relationships hold 73% of all messages, nearly three times as many as the other eight combined

claim: Memory-conditioned results rest on five subjects under the strict reading.
quote: Under the strict reading, five subjects contribute no memory-bearing probes at all, so every quantity conditioned on memory demand is a macro-average over five subjects with intervals to match, and none of them should be read as though it rested on ten.

claim: Labels were derived by language models and audited; an independent model audit found stage A's written reasoning wrong on about a fifth of rows, though reference replies disagreed on only 7 of 1,533.
quote: so close to a fifth of stage A’s written reasons are wrong, against 7 of 1,533 for the reference replies those reasons accompany.

claim: The persona layer (trait estimates, clinical-style summary) is model-produced, not a validated psychological instrument, and was never reviewed by the participants.
quote: Neither is a validated psychological instrument. Neither was administered to the subject or reviewed by them, and the release terms permit no use of either as an assessment of any person.

claim: Release terms forbid profiling, identifying or targeting individuals, any commercial use, and claims about whether the relationships helped or harmed anyone.
quote: Any claim about whether these relationships benefited or harmed anyone: the corpus records that a relationship continued, not what it did for the person in it.

claim: The dataset is gated on Hugging Face: released by Quis Inc., a person reviews every access request, and users must accept a Data Use Agreement.
quote: The dataset is released by Quis Inc. Access is controlled. You request it, a person reviews the request, and you agree to the terms on this page before you can download anything.

claim: A deployed-style memory system (the Codex port) answered 44.5% of answerable questions correctly across ten subjects.
quote: On the current release the port answers 44.5% of answerable questions correctly, macro over ten subjects, and 58.1% of chat probes.

claim: Independent prior work (CUPID, COLM 2025, peer-reviewed) also found models fail to tell which past context matters: under 50% precision.
quote: state-of-the-art LLMs struggle to infer preferences from multi-turn interactions and fail to discern what previous context is relevant to a new request -- under 50% precision and 65% recall.

claim: Independent preprint HorizonBench (simulated 6-month users) found the best of 25 frontier models at 52.8%, most at or below a 20% chance baseline, often sticking to a user's outdated preference.
quote: Across 25 frontier models, the best model reaches 52.8% and most score at or below the 20% chance baseline.

claim: Independent preprint CompanionBench, which also uses de-identified real data, found the dominant failure of companion agents is surface warmth instead of real support.
quote: Across agents, the dominant failure mode is substituting surface warmth for substantive relational support.
